summary: The note describes the Lion Capital of Ashoka, a sculpture of four Asiatic lions standing back to back on an elaborate base with other animals. It was placed by Emperor Ashoka around 250 BCE atop the Aśoka pillar at the Buddhist site of Sarnath, and is now housed in the Sarnath Museum in Uttar Pradesh. A graphic representation of the capital was adopted as the official Emblem of India in 1950, and the note compares it with other surviving Ashokan capitals.
one_line: The Lion Capital of Ashoka, a four-lion sculpture from Sarnath now in the Sarnath Museum, became India's official emblem in 1950.
key_facts: The Lion Capital of Ashoka is a sculpture of four Asiatic lions standing back to back on an elaborate base that includes other animals.
A graphic representation of the Lion Capital of Ashoka was adopted as the official Emblem of India in 1950.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka was originally placed atop the Aśoka pillar at the Buddhist site of Sarnath by the Emperor Ashoka, in about 250 BCE.
The Aśoka pillar at Sarnath is still in its original location.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka is now in the Sarnath Museum, in the state of Uttar Pradesh, India.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka stands 2.15 metres (7 feet) high including the base.
The Lion Capital is more elaborate than the other very similar surviving capitals of Ashoka's pillars bearing the Edicts of Ashoka.
The Edicts of Ashoka pillars were placed throughout India, and several of their capitals feature single animals at the top.
One other damaged group of four lions survives, at Sanchi.
